claim: The adult frog retina retains a reservoir of active neural stem cells that contribute to continuous eye growth throughout life.
source: The adult frog retina retains a reservoir of active neural stem cells that contribute to continuous eye growth throughout life.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a background fact about the model system being studied.

claim: Yap is specifically expressed in retinal stem cells.
source: We found that Yap, a downstream effector of the Hippo pathway, is specifically expressed in these stem cells.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunostaining data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Yap knock-down leads to an accelerated S-phase.
source: Yap knock-down leads to an accelerated S-phase and an abnormal progression of DNA replication, a phenotype likely mediated by upregulation of c-Myc.
evidence: Supported by cumulative labeling assays and EdU-labeled replication foci analysis in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Yap knock-down leads to abnormal progression of DNA replication.
source: Yap knock-down leads to an accelerated S-phase and an abnormal progression of DNA replication, a phenotype likely mediated by upregulation of c-Myc.
evidence: Supported by analysis of replication foci patterns showing decreased late S-phase patterns in Figure 5.

claim: The S-phase acceleration phenotype is likely mediated by upregulation of c-Myc.
source: Yap knock-down leads to an accelerated S-phase and an abnormal progression of DNA replication, a phenotype likely mediated by upregulation of c-Myc.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and qPCR showing c-Myc upregulation in Yap morphants (Figure 5), combined with literature on c-Myc's role in S-phase acceleration.

claim: Yap knock-down is associated with an increased occurrence of DNA damage.
source: This is associated with an increased occurrence of DNA damage and eventually p53-p21 pathway-mediated cell death.
evidence: Supported by γ-H2AX immunolabeling showing increased DNA double-strand breaks in Figure 7.

claim: Yap knock-down leads to p53-p21 pathway-mediated cell death.
source: This is associated with an increased occurrence of DNA damage and eventually p53-p21 pathway-mediated cell death.
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assays showing increased apoptosis and in situ hybridization/NanoString showing p53 and p21 upregulation in Figure 7.

claim: PKNOX1 is a transcription factor involved in the maintenance of genomic stability.
source: Finally, we identified PKNOX1, a transcription factor involved in the maintenance of genomic stability, as a functional and physical interactant of YAP.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Iotti et al., 2011) mentioned in the Introduction.

claim: PKNOX1 is a functional and physical interactant of YAP.
source: Finally, we identified PKNOX1, a transcription factor involved in the maintenance of genomic stability, as a functional and physical interactant of YAP.
evidence: Supported by BiFC and co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 8, and functional interaction studies in Figure 9.

claim: YAP is required in adult retinal stem cells to regulate the temporal firing of replication origins.
source: Altogether, we propose that YAP is required in adult retinal stem cells to regulate the temporal firing of replication origins and quality control of replicated DNA.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed S-phase shortening and altered replication foci patterns upon Yap knockdown.

claim: YAP is required in adult retinal stem cells for quality control of replicated DNA.
source: Altogether, we propose that YAP is required in adult retinal stem cells to regulate the temporal firing of replication origins and quality control of replicated DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased DNA damage observed upon Yap knockdown.

claim: Specific mechanisms dedicated to S-phase control are at work in stem cells to protect them from genomic instability.
source: Our data reinforce the view that specific mechanisms dedicated to S-phase control are at work in stem cells to protect them from genomic instability.
evidence: This is a broader conclusion drawn from the findings about YAP's role in S-phase regulation and genomic stability.

claim: The ciliary marginal zone (CMZ) contains genuine multipotent and self-renewing neural stem cells.
source: In the fish or amphibian retina, a continuously proliferating peripheral domain called ciliary marginal zone (CMZ) (Wetts et al., 1989; Perron et al., 1998) was recently formally demonstrated to contain genuine multipotent and self-renewing neural stem cells (Centanin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Centanin et al., 2011.

claim: The CMZ ensures cell replacement and contributes to life-long growth of the eye through permanent generation of all retinal cell types.
source: The CMZ not only ensures cell replacement, but also contributes to life-long growth of the eye through the permanent generation of all retinal cell types.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the CMZ.

claim: YAP was identified as a major regulator of organ growth through its actions on embryonic precursor cells.
source: The Hippo pathway effector yes-associated protein (YAP) was identified as a major regulator of organ growth through its actions on embryonic precursor cells (Lian et al., 2010; Ramos and Camargo, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lian et al., 2010 and Ramos and Camargo, 2012.

claim: Yap overexpression increases self-renewal of airway basal stem cells.
source: For instance, Yap overexpression increases self-renewal of airway basal stem cells (Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2014.

claim: Yap overexpression leads to a loss of intestinal stem cells.
source: In contrast, it surprisingly leads to a loss of intestinal stem cells (Barry et al., 2013), while being seemingly neutral regarding the quantity and function of hematopoietic stem cells (Jansson and Larsson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barry et al., 2013.

claim: Yap overexpression is seemingly neutral regarding the quantity and function of hematopoietic stem cells.
source: In contrast, it surprisingly leads to a loss of intestinal stem cells (Barry et al., 2013), while being seemingly neutral regarding the quantity and function of hematopoietic stem cells (Jansson and Larsson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jansson and Larsson, 2012.

claim: YAP is largely dispensable in a physiological context for the homeostasis of several adult organs.
source: Inactivation studies further suggested that YAP is largely dispensable in a physiological context for the homeostasis of several adult organs (Cai et al., 2010; Azzolin et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014), although this might reflect in some cases functional redundancy with the other Hippo effector TAZ (Imajo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cai et al., 2010; Azzolin et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: YAP dispensability in adult organs might reflect functional redundancy with TAZ.
source: Inactivation studies further suggested that YAP is largely dispensable in a physiological context for the homeostasis of several adult organs (Cai et al., 2010; Azzolin et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014), although this might reflect in some cases functional redundancy with the other Hippo effector TAZ (Imajo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Imajo et al., 2015.

claim: Yap expression is prominent in the presumptive retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) and in the neural retina/RPE border at the optic vesicle stage.
source: In situ hybridization at the optic vesicle stage revealed prominent Yap expression in the presumptive retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) and in the neural retina/RPE border (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), a region we previously proposed to be the presumptive adult stem cell niche (El Yakoubi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The neural retina/RPE border region was previously proposed to be the presumptive adult stem cell niche.
source: In situ hybridization at the optic vesicle stage revealed prominent Yap expression in the presumptive retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) and in the neural retina/RPE border (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), a region we previously proposed to be the presumptive adult stem cell niche (El Yakoubi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to El Yakoubi et al., 2012.

claim: In the post-embryonic retina, Yap is expressed in the most peripheral stem cell-containing region of the CMZ.
source: In line with this, we found that in the post-embryonic retina, Yap is expressed in the most peripheral stem cell-containing region of the CMZ (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: YAP protein is detected in stem cells located at the tip of the CMZ, mainly in the cytoplasm, although some signal is observed in the nuclei.
source: YAP protein was detected in stem cells located at the tip of the CMZ, mainly in the cytoplasm, although some signal could be observed as well in the nuclei of these cells.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: YAP is found in Müller glial cells.
source: Of note, we also found YAP labeling in Müller glial cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Yap staining is prominent in EdU-negative stem cells and in the most peripheral EdU-positive cells (young progenitors).
source: Yap staining was found to be prominent in EdU-negative stem cells and in the most peripheral EdU-positive cells (young progenitors).
evidence: Supported by EdU labeling and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Yap staining wanes in more central older progenitor cells.
source: The staining then waned in more central older progenitor cells.
evidence: Supported by EdU labeling and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Taz is faintly expressed in the post-embryonic retina and only a weak and diffuse signal is detected in the CMZ.
source: Of note, in contrast to Yap, Taz is faintly expressed in the post-embryonic retina and only a weak and diffuse signal could be detected in the CMZ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both Tead1 and Tead2 are expressed in the periphery of the CMZ where Yap is expressed.
source: We found consistent labeling of both Tead1 and Tead2 in the periphery of the CMZ where Yap is expressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Yap-overexpressing tadpoles display eye overgrowth on the injected side.
source: Yap-overexpressing tadpoles displayed eye overgrowth on the injected side (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Yap overexpression results in a decreased number of TUNEL-positive cells.
source: We found that Yap overexpression results in both a decreased number of TUNEL-positive cells (Figure 1G,H) and a dramatic expansion of the EdU-positive cell population (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: Yap overexpression results in a dramatic expansion of the EdU-positive cell population.
source: We found that Yap overexpression results in both a decreased number of TUNEL-positive cells (Figure 1G,H) and a dramatic expansion of the EdU-positive cell population (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: The overproliferative phenotype is strongly exacerbated upon overexpression of YapS98A mutant.
source: The overproliferative phenotype was strongly exacerbated upon overexpression of a Yap mutant construct where Ser-98 was replaced by an alanine (YapS98A) (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Ser-98 in Xenopus YAP (Ser-127 in mammalian YAP) is a conserved Lats phosphorylation site that mediates the growth-suppressive output of the Hippo signaling cascade in vivo.
source: This residue (Ser-127 in mammalian YAP) is a conserved Lats phosphorylation site that has been shown to mediate the growth-suppressive output of the Hippo signaling cascade in vivo (Zhao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2007.

claim: Overexpression of YapΔTBS (lacking the TEAD binding site) is unable to trigger enhanced proliferation in the CMZ.
source: In contrast, overexpression of a truncated construct lacking the TEAD binding site (YapΔTBS) was unable to trigger enhanced proliferation in the CMZ, suggesting that the overproliferative phenotype requires interaction with a TEAD protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Yap-dependent overproliferative phenotype requires interaction with a TEAD protein.
source: In contrast, overexpression of a truncated construct lacking the TEAD binding site (YapΔTBS) was unable to trigger enhanced proliferation in the CMZ, suggesting that the overproliferative phenotype requires interaction with a TEAD protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that YapΔTBS does not cause overproliferation.

claim: Yap-dependent retinal overgrowth is likely caused by enhanced cell survival and cell proliferation.
source: Together, these data reveal that Yap-dependent retinal overgrowth is likely caused by enhanced cell survival and cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased TUNEL-positive cells and increased EdU-positive cells.

claim: Yap morphant tadpoles exhibit significantly reduced eye size compared to controls.
source: In these conditions, morphant tadpoles developed but exhibited significantly reduced eye size compared to controls (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The Yap-MO small eye phenotype is restored upon co-injection of Yap-MO with non-targetable Yap mRNAs.
source: Importantly, this phenotype was restored upon co-injection of Yap-MO with non-targetable Yap mRNAs, demonstrating specificity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Yap knockdown effects on eye size are eye autonomous.
source: When the optic vesicle of a control tailbud was transplanted into an enucleated morphant embryo, it nevertheless reached a normal size. In contrast, Yap-MO optic vesicles grafted in a control host generated smaller eyes, which is in accordance with Yap knockdown effects being eye autonomous.
evidence: Supported by optic vesicle transplantation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Restoring YAP function at late embryogenesis, following knockdown during development, leads to tadpoles with normal sized eyes.
source: We found that restoring YAP function at late embryogenesis, following knockdown during development, leads to tadpoles with normal sized eyes (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: Supported by photo-MO experiments shown in Figure 3B–D.

claim: The Yap-MO phenotype is not the indirect consequence of developmental morphogenetic defects.
source: This supports the hypothesis that the Yap-MO phenotype is not the indirect consequence of developmental morphogenetic defects.
evidence: This is inferred from the photo-MO rescue experiments.

claim: Conditional Yap knockdown starting at late retinogenesis is sufficient to trigger a small eye phenotype.
source: In line with this, conditional Yap knockdown starting at late retinogenesis was found to be sufficient to trigger a small eye phenotype (Figure 3B,E,F).
evidence: Supported by inducible photo-MO experiments shown in Figure 3B,E,F.

claim: YAP has a specific role in the homeostatic control of post-embryonic retinal growth.
source: Together, these data point to a specific role for YAP in the homeostatic control of post-embryonic retinal growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the photo-MO experiments showing that Yap is required specifically during post-embryonic stages.

claim: Yap-MO-injected tadpoles harbor a significantly decreased number of EdU+ cells in the CMZ compared to controls.
source: Yap-MO-injected tadpoles harbored a significantly decreased number of EdU+ cells compared to a control situation (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The difference in EdU-labeling between control and Yap morphant tadpoles is more pronounced at the tip of the CMZ where stem cells reside.
source: The difference in EdU-labeling between control and Yap morphant tadpoles was even more pronounced at the tip of the CMZ where stem cells reside and Yap expression is the strongest (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Both stem and progenitor cell populations are still present in Yap-MO-injected tadpoles.
source: Using in situ hybridization, we examined the expression of several retinal stem and progenitor cell markers (Figure 2F and data not shown). Surprisingly, stainings observed in Yap-MO-injected tadpoles were similar to control ones, indicating that both stem and progenitor cell populations were still present.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Neither the total number of cells within the CMZ nor the size of the proliferative cell population (PCNA labeled) is significantly affected by Yap knockdown.
source: Accordingly, neither the total number of cells within the CMZ nor the size of the proliferative cell population (PCNA labeled) was significantly affected (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: Supported by Hoechst and PCNA staining data shown in Figure 2G–J.

claim: Yap knockdown does not induce stem/progenitor cell exhaustion but rather alters the relative proportion of time these cells spend in S-phase of the cell cycle.
source: Together, these data indicate that Yap knockdown does not induce stem/progenitor cell exhaustion but rather alters the relative proportion of time these cells spend in S-phase of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that stem/progenitor markers are present but EdU incorporation is reduced.

claim: Yap knockdown results in a significantly lower percentage of mitotic cells per section in the CMZ compared to control.
source: We found that compared to the control, Yap knockdown results in a significantly lower percentage of mitotic cells per section, which is suggestive of a longer total cell cycle length.
evidence: Supported by PH3 immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The lower mitotic index in Yap morphants is suggestive of a longer total cell cycle length.
source: We found that compared to the control, Yap knockdown results in a significantly lower percentage of mitotic cells per section, which is suggestive of a longer total cell cycle length.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased mitotic index.

claim: The PLM is consistently lower at each time point in Yap morphant retinas compared to control ones, indicating a delayed S- to M-phase progression.
source: Noticeably, the PLM was consistently lower at each time point in Yap morphant retinas compared to control ones, indicating a delayed S- to M-phase progression.
evidence: Supported by PLM experiment data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The mean G2 length (TG2) doubled in Yap morphant retinas compared to the control (from approximately 2.5 to 4.5 hr).
source: We estimated that the mean G2 length (TG2; see 'Materials and methods' for details) doubled in Yap morphant retinas compared to the control (from approximately 2.5 to 4.5 hr).
evidence: Supported by PLM experiment data and calculations shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Yap knockdown results in perturbed cell cycle kinetics within the CMZ.
source: It thus appears that Yap knockdown results in perturbed cell cycle kinetics within the CMZ.
evidence: This is inferred from the mitotic index and PLM data.

claim: The labeling index in the linear part of the cumulative labeling curve is consistently lower in Yap morphant retinal stem cells compared to control ones.
source: As shown in Figure 4F, the labeling index in the linear part of the curve was consistently lower in Yap morphant retinal stem cells compared to control ones.
evidence: Supported by cumulative labeling assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Calculation of TC confirmed the hypothesis of extended cell cycle duration following Yap-Mo injection.
source: Calculation of TC confirmed the hypothesis of extended cell cycle duration following Yap-Mo injection.
evidence: Supported by cumulative labeling assay data and calculations shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Yap knockdown revealed a dramatic reduction of S-phase length in morphant retinal stem cells.
source: Surprisingly, it also revealed a dramatic reduction of S-phase length in morphant cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by cumulative labeling assay data and calculations shown in Figure 4G.

claim: c-Myc accelerates S-phase by inducing premature origin firing initiation and increasing origin density.
source: The c-Myc proto-oncogene has been shown to accelerate S-phase by inducing premature origin firing initiation and increasing origin density (Robinson et al., 2009; Srinivasan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Robinson et al., 2009 and Srinivasan et al., 2013.

claim: In situ hybridization and qPCR analyses revealed an upregulation and expansion of c-Myc expression in the CMZ of the Yap morphant retina.
source: In situ hybridization and qPCR analyses revealed an upregulation and expansion of c-Myc expression in the CMZ of the Yap morphant retina (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and qPCR data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: c-Myc upregulation may account, at least in part, for the S-phase length shortening in Yap morphants.
source: This may account, at least in part, for the S-phase length shortening.
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of c-Myc in S-phase acceleration and its upregulation in Yap morphants.

claim: In the control situation, both early and late replication patterns are found within the stem cell population of the CMZ.
source: In the control situation, we found both early and late patterns within the stem cell population of the CMZ.
evidence: Supported by EdU-labeled replication foci analysis shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: The proportion of cells in mid/late S-phase is dramatically reduced in Yap morphant cells.
source: In contrast, the proportion of cells in mid/late S-phase was dramatically reduced in Yap morphant cells (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Supported by EdU-labeled replication foci analysis shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Loss of YAP function in retinal stem cells alters their temporal program of DNA replication.
source: Altogether, these data highlight that loss of YAP function in retinal stem cells alters their temporal program of DNA replication and points to c-Myc as a potential actor in this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the altered replication foci patterns and c-Myc upregulation.

claim: c-Myc is a potential actor in the alteration of DNA replication timing caused by YAP loss.
source: Altogether, these data highlight that loss of YAP function in retinal stem cells alters their temporal program of DNA replication and points to c-Myc as a potential actor in this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the c-Myc upregulation and its known role in S-phase regulation.

claim: A similar phenotype (decrease in late replication patterns and c-Myc up-regulation) is observed in the ventricular zone of the neural tube where Yap is expressed.
source: Interestingly, a similar phenotype (decrease in late replication patterns and c-Myc up-regulation) was also observed in the ventricular zone of the neural tube where Yap is expressed, suggesting that YAP function in S-phase progression may also hold true in other neural precursor cells (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6A–D.

claim: YAP function in S-phase progression may hold true in other neural precursor cells beyond retinal stem cells.
source: Interestingly, a similar phenotype (decrease in late replication patterns and c-Myc up-regulation) was also observed in the ventricular zone of the neural tube where Yap is expressed, suggesting that YAP function in S-phase progression may also hold true in other neural precursor cells (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar phenotype observed in the neural tube.

claim: The number of γ-H2AX-positive cells is significantly increased in Yap-MO-injected CMZ compared to controls.
source: The number of γ-H2AX-positive cells was significantly increased in Yap-MO-injected CMZ compared to controls (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by γ-H2AX immunolabeling data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Cell death is severely increased in Yap morphant retinas.
source: Since extensive DNA damage may trigger apoptosis, we next turned to a TUNEL assay and found that cell death was indeed severely increased in morphant retinas (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: The majority of apoptotic cells in Yap morphants is found at 'the exit' of the CMZ close to the neural retina, not in the most peripheral part where Yap is expressed.
source: Surprisingly, the majority of apoptotic cells was found at 'the exit' of the CMZ close to the neural retina, and not in its most peripheral part where Yap is expressed.
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Apoptosis in Yap morphants occurs as a secondary consequence in late progenitor cells generated from stem cells that experienced YAP function inhibition.
source: This strongly suggests that apoptosis occurs as a secondary consequence in late progenitor cells generated from stem cells that experienced YAP function inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial distribution of apoptotic cells.

claim: Fewer neurons are generated in a 2-day period in Yap morphant retinas compared to control ones.
source: As expected, we found that fewer neurons were generated in a 2-day period in Yap morphant retinas compared to control ones (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by EdU chase experiment data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: Among 15 cell cycle genes analyzed, only p53 and p21 were significantly affected by Yap knockdown, with much higher levels in Yap morphant retinas.
source: Among them, only p53 and p21Cip1/WAF1 (previously named Xic2 in Xenopus and p21 hereafter) were significantly affected, with much higher levels present in Yap morphant retinas compared to control ones (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by NanoString analysis data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: p53 expression in the wild type retina is restricted to the CMZ.
source: In situ hybridization analysis revealed that its expression in the wild type retina is restricted to the CMZ.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: p53 staining is strongly enhanced in the CMZ of Yap-MO-injected tadpoles.
source: In addition and consistent with the NanoString data, p53 staining was strongly enhanced in the CMZ of Yap-MO-injected tadpoles (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: p53 is up-regulated in the neural tube of Yap morphants.
source: Of note, an up-regulation was observed in the neural tube as well (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: p21 is a member of the CIP/KIP family of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors that blocks the G1-S transition.
source: p21 is a member of the CIP/KIP family of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors that blocks the G1-S transition and has emerged as a key player in the p53 pathway (Attardi and DePinho, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Attardi and DePinho, 2004.

claim: p21 has emerged as a key player in the p53 pathway.
source: p21 is a member of the CIP/KIP family of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors that blocks the G1-S transition and has emerged as a key player in the p53 pathway (Attardi and DePinho, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Attardi and DePinho, 2004.

claim: Strong ectopic p21 labeling is observed within the CMZ of Yap morphant tadpoles.
source: We thus performed in situ hybridization and observed a strong ectopic p21 labeling within the CMZ of Yap morphant tadpoles (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Increased apoptosis and delayed cell cycle progression resulting from Yap knockdown might be driven by the p53-p21 pathway.
source: As a whole, these results suggest that increased apoptosis and probably delayed cell cycle progression resulting from Yap knockdown might be driven by the p53-p21 pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the upregulation of p53 and p21 and their known functions.

claim: YAP and PKNOX1 interact in vitro using a two-hybrid assay.
source: We found that the two proteins indeed interact in vitro using a two-hybrid assay (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: Co-transfection of Yap and Tead1 constructs results in a significant nuclear BiFC signal.
source: As expected, co-transfection of Yap and Tead1 constructs resulted in a significant nuclear BiFC signal.
evidence: Supported by BiFC experiment data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The YAP/TEAD1 BiFC signal is lost using a YapΔTBS mutant devoid of TEAD binding site, validating the specificity of the BiFC staining.
source: This was lost using a Yap∆TBS mutant devoid of TEAD binding site, validating the specificity of the BiFC staining.
evidence: Supported by BiFC experiment data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Co-transfection of both Yap and pknox1 constructs leads to a positive BiFC signal that mainly localizes to the cytoplasm.
source: Co-transfection of both Yap and pknox1 constructs led to a positive BiFC signal that mainly localized to the cytoplasm.
evidence: Supported by BiFC experiment data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: YAP/PKNOX1 interaction is confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation analyses following expression of tagged proteins.
source: YAP/PKNOX1 interaction was further confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation analyses following expression of tagged proteins (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: pknox1 is expressed in the CMZ.
source: Since we found that pknox1 is expressed in the CMZ (Figure 9A), we next sought for potential functional interaction with YAP in retinal stem cells.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: pknox1 knockdown leads to a significant reduction in total eye size.
source: Although the eye phenotype appeared more dramatic than that observed upon Yap knockdown (layering defects of the retina), it similarly led to a significant reduction in total eye size (Figure 9B,C), associated with decreased EdU incorporation in the CMZ compared to controls (Figure 9G,H).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 9B,C.

claim: pknox1 knockdown is associated with decreased EdU incorporation in the CMZ compared to controls.
source: Although the eye phenotype appeared more dramatic than that observed upon Yap knockdown (layering defects of the retina), it similarly led to a significant reduction in total eye size (Figure 9B,C), associated with decreased EdU incorporation in the CMZ compared to controls (Figure 9G,H).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 9G,H.

claim: Analysis of EdU-labeled replication foci revealed a decreased proportion of stem cells in mid/late S-phase in pknox1 morphants.
source: In addition, analysis of EdU-labeled replication foci revealed a decreased proportion of stem cells in mid/late S-phase (Figure 9D–E) in pknox1 morphant, as observed following Yap knockdown.
evidence: Supported by EdU-labeled replication foci analysis shown in Figure 9D–E.

claim: pknox1 morphants display upregulation of c-Myc expression in the CMZ.
source: These embryos also displayed upregulation of c-Myc expression in the CMZ, thus recapitulating main features of the Yap knockdown phenotype (Figure 9F).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: pknox1 overexpression alone does not significantly affect CMZ cell proliferation.
source: Of note, pknox1 overexpression alone does not significantly affect CMZ cell proliferation.
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 9I,J.

claim: pknox1 mRNA injection exacerbates Yap gain of function phenotype.
source: In these conditions, pknox1 mRNA injection was found to exacerbate Yap gain of function phenotype (Figure 9I,J).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 9I,J.

claim: pknox1 knockdown rescues the overproliferative effects of Yap misexpression.
source: Finally, we tested whether pknox1 knockdown might rescue the overproliferative effects of Yap misexpression. We found indeed that EdU incorporation was restored to a basal level in a pknox1 morphant context (Figure 9K,L).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 9K,L.

claim: PKNOX1 physically and functionally interacts with YAP in the CMZ.
source: Together, these data support the idea that PKNOX1 physically and functionally interacts with YAP in the CMZ.
evidence: This is inferred from the BiFC, co-IP, and functional interaction data.

claim: YAP is dispensable for the maintenance of the stem cell pool in adult organs.
source: As observed in other adult organs in mammals (Azzolin et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014), our results suggest that YAP is dispensable for the maintenance of the stem cell pool.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that stem cells are still present in Yap morphants, and supported by citations.

claim: YAP depletion lengthens retinal stem cell divisions.
source: We instead uncovered that its depletion lengthens retinal stem cell divisions.
evidence: This is supported by the cumulative labeling assay data showing increased TC.

claim: YAP depletion is associated with a dramatic shortening of S-phase in retinal stem cells.
source: However, to our surprise, this is associated with a dramatic shortening of their S-phase.
evidence: This is supported by the cumulative labeling assay data showing decreased TS.

claim: Yap knockdown results in a marked reduction of late S-phase labeling patterns, suggesting that some firing origins have advanced their activation timing.
source: Our observation that Yap knockdown results in a mark reduction of late S-phase labeling patterns can suggest that some firing origins have advanced their activation timing, which may account for the reduced S-phase duration.
evidence: This is inferred from the replication foci analysis data.

claim: c-Myc overexpression causes increased replication origin activity and consequent S-phase shortening.
source: Its overexpression indeed causes increased replication origin activity and consequent S-phase shortening (Dominguez-Sola et al., 2007; Robinson et al., 2009; Srinivasan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dominguez-Sola et al., 2007; Robinson et al., 2009; Srinivasan et al., 2013.

claim: In Drosophila or cancer cells, c-Myc has been reported to be positively regulated by Yap.
source: Intriguingly, in contrast to Drosophila or cancer cells, where c-Myc has been reported to be positively regulated by Yap (Neto-Silva et al., 2010; Stocker, 2011; Xiao et al., 2013), we found that its expression is enhanced in the CMZ of Yap morphant tadpoles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Neto-Silva et al., 2010; Stocker, 2011; Xiao et al., 2013.

claim: YAP may regulate replication origin licencing in G1.
source: Besides, in addition to be involved in replication progression, we do not exclude that YAP may also regulate replication origin licencing in G1, as recently reported in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (Shen and Stanger, 2015).
evidence: This is speculative, based on a citation to Shen and Stanger, 2015.

claim: Delayed G-phase progression in Yap morphants might occur as a secondary consequence of S-phase defects.
source: Alternatively, delayed G-phase progression might occur as a secondary consequence of S-phase defects.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism.

claim: Replication stress is a source of DNA damage, which may ultimately trigger activation of the p53-p21 pathway.
source: Replication stress is a source of DNA damage, which may ultimately trigger activation of the p53-p21 pathway (Bartek and Lukas, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bartek and Lukas, 2001.

claim: c-Myc overexpression in vitro leads to increased occurrence of double-strand breaks.
source: As observed following c-Myc overexpression in vitro (Dominguez-Sola et al., 2007; Robinson et al., 2009; Srinivasan et al., 2013), we found an increased occurrence of double-strand breaks in Yap morphant retina, associated with an upregulation of both p53 and p21.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dominguez-Sola et al., 2007; Robinson et al., 2009; Srinivasan et al., 2013.

claim: p21 is known to inhibit G1/S and G2/M transitions.
source: Since p21 is known to inhibit G1/S and G2/M transitions and p53 to induce programmed cell death (Vogelstein et al., 2000), this could contribute to both the lengthening in G phases and the increased number of apoptotic cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vogelstein et al., 2000.

claim: p53 is known to induce programmed cell death.
source: Since p21 is known to inhibit G1/S and G2/M transitions and p53 to induce programmed cell death (Vogelstein et al., 2000), this could contribute to both the lengthening in G phases and the increased number of apoptotic cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vogelstein et al., 2000.

claim: Mammalian cortical neural stem cells exhibit a substantially longer S-phase than progenitors committed to neuron production.
source: Regarding cell cycle progression, it has been shown during development that mammalian cortical neural stem cells exhibit a substantially longer S-phase than progenitors committed to neuron production (Arai et al., 2011; Turrero García et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arai et al., 2011 and Turrero García et al., 2015.

claim: Neural stem cells may need to invest more time during S-phase into quality control of replicated DNA.
source: It was thus proposed that neural stem cells may need to invest more time during S-phase into quality control of replicated DNA.
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis based on the longer S-phase in neural stem cells.

claim: CMZ retinal stem cells exhibit a longer S-phase compared to fast amplifying progenitors.
source: In agreement with this, we also found that CMZ retinal stem cells exhibit a longer S-phase compared to fast amplifying progenitors (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: YAP may be critically involved in stem cell specific regulation of S-phase.
source: In addition, our work points for the first time towards a factor, YAP, that may be critically involved in this stem cell specific regulation of S-phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings about YAP's role in S-phase regulation.

claim: YAP appears to be required for proper choreography of the DNA replication program.
source: Although its precise function in this process remains to be investigated, it indeed appears to be required for proper choreography of the DNA replication program and may as such be necessary to maintain genomic integrity of retinal stem cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the altered replication timing and increased DNA damage upon YAP loss.

claim: YAP may be necessary to maintain genomic integrity of retinal stem cells.
source: Although its precise function in this process remains to be investigated, it indeed appears to be required for proper choreography of the DNA replication program and may as such be necessary to maintain genomic integrity of retinal stem cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased DNA damage upon YAP loss.

claim: Aberrant DNA replication timing has been proposed to be a causative factor in diseases such as cancer and neuronal disorders.
source: Our findings also have important medical implications since aberrant DNA replication timing has been proposed to be a causative factor in diseases such as cancer and neuronal disorders (Aladjem, 2007; Watanabe and Maekawa, 2010; Donley and Thayer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aladjem, 2007; Watanabe and Maekawa, 2010; Donley and Thayer, 2013.

claim: LATS1 has been involved in ATR-mediated response to replication stress in lung cancer cells.
source: Interestingly, another component of the Hippo pathway, LATS1, has very recently been involved in ATR-mediated response to replication stress in lung cancer cells (Pefani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pefani et al., 2014.

claim: Several Hippo pathway components may regulate S-phase progression and quality control and thereby safeguard genomic integrity.
source: Several Hippo pathway components may thus regulate (independently or in concert) S-phase progression and quality control and thereby safeguard genomic integrity.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings about YAP and LATS1.

claim: Homothorax partners the Drosophila Yap homologue Yorkie in some developmental contexts.
source: Although Homothorax is known to partner the Drosophila Yap homologue Yorkie in some developmental contexts (Peng et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2011), this has not been reported yet for its vertebrate orthologs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2009 and Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: PKNOX1 belongs to the TALE (three amino acids loop extension) class of homeodomain proteins.
source: PKNOX1 belongs to the TALE (three amino acids loop extension) class of homeodomain proteins and is involved in many developmental processes (Berthelsen et al., 1998; Ferretti et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berthelsen et al., 1998 and Ferretti et al., 2006.

claim: PKNOX1 is involved in many developmental processes.
source: PKNOX1 belongs to the TALE (three amino acids loop extension) class of homeodomain proteins and is involved in many developmental processes (Berthelsen et al., 1998; Ferretti et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berthelsen et al., 1998 and Ferretti et al., 2006.

claim: Down-regulation of pknox1 in both zebrafish and mouse embryos leads to a small eye phenotype.
source: Down-regulation of pknox1 in both zebrafish and mouse embryos leads to a small eye phenotype (Deflorian et al., 2004; Ferretti et al., 2006), reminiscent of what we found in Xenopus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deflorian et al., 2004 and Ferretti et al., 2006.

claim: pknox1 inactivation triggers cell death in the zebrafish CNS.
source: Interestingly, pknox1 inactivation was reported to trigger cell death in the zebrafish CNS (Deflorian et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deflorian et al., 2004.

claim: pknox1 deficiency leads to increased DNA damage and apoptosis both in embryonic fibroblasts and in the mouse epiblast.
source: Furthermore, pknox1 deficiency leads to increased DNA damage and apoptosis both in embryonic fibroblasts and in the mouse epiblast (Micali et al., 2009; Fernandez-Diaz et al., 2010; Iotti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Micali et al., 2009; Fernandez-Diaz et al., 2010; Iotti et al., 2011.

claim: PKNOX1 and YAP interact together to maintain genomic stability in retinal stem cells.
source: On the basis of these different reports and our findings, we thus propose that PKNOX1 and YAP interact together to maintain genomic stability in retinal stem cells.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and literature.
